speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today at the request of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General of
Canada, my Hon. colleague for Megantic-Compton- Stanstead (Mr. Gerin), whom I view as someone vigourously and strenuously defending his convictions and those of his constituents. I would like briefly, in view of the time at my disposal, to discuss the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), to amend the Criminal Code to grant "whistleblowers" a certain immunity from prosecution. I will therefore take some time to look with other Hon. Members for a solution to the problem of leaks by public servants in the federal Government.
First, Madam Speaker, we must give serious consideration to the reasons why an employee or a public servant may act against his superiors or his employer. Such a public servant who betrays his oath of office and confidentiality surely must face a grave problem of conscience and professional ethics. A leak may not be the best form of denunciation. Disclosure by a public servant who sees no other way, but who also may know only part of the facts, could seriously embarrass the Government and even cause irreparable damage to innocent people. Where newspapermen are concerned, you will notice that increasingly they tend to check their sources and are very reluctant to disclose information based on rumours or more or less convincing evidence. On the other hand, others might view leaks as an effective control over bureaucracy and even legislators.
We could also ask ourselves how such a procedure is viewed by the public. I think people have conflicting feelings in that respect. Some will feel outraged at such misconduct by "whistleblowers", while others will be relieved to know there are some watchful people who stay alert and blow the whistle.
I see that my time is running out. What I would propose is perhaps the appointment of an ombudsman, with the power needed to do his work. Of course, opponents will say that we are only adding to an already huge bureaucracy and will only succeed in compounding and multiplying problems. My answer is that fire is best fought with fire. Water is best fought with water, and bureaucracy and its abuse are best fought by yet an additional bureaucratic level.
As I said, Madam Speaker, the solution does not lie in an amendment to the Criminal Code to protect "whistleblowers" against harassment, persecution and prosecution. It lies rather in the strength of an independant ombudsman who could deal confidentially with complaints and who will expose wrongdoings after a responsible enquiry has proved there was wrongdoing.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I appreciate that. I was saying that there are some areas I wish to cover that have been debated in the House. The first issue with which I would like to deal is the issue of sovereignty.
In my view, a trade negotiation is an exercise in sovereignty, not in surrender. All trade negotiations involve commitments made by participants with the understanding that arrangements can be terminated by any of the principals prepared to suffer the consequences. As such, there is no loss of sovereignty but rather its use through an agreed exchange. If I may, I would like to give a couple of examples of this.
In 1935, Canada and the United States successfully negotiated a bilateral trade agreement which lowered tariffs on each country's products. Subsequently, Canada, in a series of GATT rounds, negotiated agreements which lowered barriers to our trade. In doing so, we also agreed to limit the use of our sovereign power by subsidizing exports, by discriminating against foreign-made products through our tax system, by raising tariffs or by purchasing non-competitive Canadian products through federal procurements. That was part of the agreement made at that time. We gave something up to get something and that is the history of trade agreements.
I contend that simply belonging to GATT and following its rules means that a country gives up a little of its sovereignty, but it does that through trade agreements. Today we are
discussing a trade agreement signed between two sovereign countries. Had the countervail gone through, I might be arguig on the other side of this issue. I might be arguing that some of our sovereignty was lost, because under the American countervail law the Americans have unilateral powers. In addition to the industries opposition, I want to quote the detailed reactions of the Canadian Paperworkers Union which represents 65,000 men and women across Canada. This union indicates that it studied the agreement very carefully. It strongly believes:
that such an agreement threatens the livelihood of our membership in the lumber sector- The agreement not only endangers jobs in the sector but also dramatically illustrates the untenable position of the Mulroney Government in its talks with the United States on the issue of free trade.
Let us be very clear that it is not only industry but a major part of the trade union movement in the country which stands with us and many newspapers across the country which have opposed this agreement. There is a widely and deeply felt opposition to what is seen as a massive sellout of the hopes of the country and our economic independence. The Conservative Government is trying, not only to force this legislation through, but to force it through by cutting off debate. I say shame and I am sure the country says shame as well.

Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me the honour of speaking in this debate. This is my second opportunity to do so this week. As the saying goes, the speech gets better the second time around. I was hoping that we would have an opportunity to hear clarification of this abominable piece of legislation from government Members. Unfortunately, they have been plagued for the past while with severe and traumatic psychological depressions and, therefore, have not been able to rouse themselves to the full fervor of an explanation, which I know they would otherwise like to provide.
Earlier today my colleague from York South-Weston talked about Shakespeare and quoted Hamlet most eloquently. That brought to mind how much we in Canada need Shakespeare to describe the present Government. When the free trade initiative was first launched Government members were full of hosannas. They paraded out on the streets that this was going to be the salvation of Canada. Shakespeare spoke of the seven stages of man. With regard to the first stage he said:
-the lover, sighing like a furnace with a woeful ballad made to his mistress' eyebrow.
That was certainly the position of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). He was singing a ballad to his mistress' eyebrow, telling us all what a furnace of affection he would have for the Americans as he brought about free trade.
Watching the face of the Prime Minister yesterday brought to mind the second stage of man as Shakespeare expressed it. He said:
-the whining schoolboy with his satchel and shining morning face creeping like snail unwillingly to school.
Only Shakespeare could describe our Prime Minister in such eloquent terms, going from the woleful lover to the schoolboy sneaking like a snail as he went, cap-in-hand, to the American vice-president supplicating to save his political skin.
January 22, 1987

You, Madam Speaker, have had the peculiar honour of having to listen to a large part of this debate. The Government justifies this legislation by saying that the stock market has gone up. I see that we can now create public policy based upon what speculators on the stock market think is right. On that basis, of course, we should be paying great homage to all those who are involved in the amalgamations, take-overs, junk bonds and other finaglings. They are now the decision makers on Tory policy.
Their other argument was that this legislation is going to be of great assistance to the industry. They find a remote quote from someone they found deep in the depths of a Fraser type think tank who says this is a wonderful thing. The Government is still financing groups of reactionary right wing brain trusts which run around the country and appear on Canada AM telling us how the particular and peculiar policies on this continent will serve us well.
We listened to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary tonight. Was that not wonderful? He said that we should not ask the Government for explanations, that that was up to the provinces. He said the Government is doing this only to give the money to the provinces. Although there is a letter from the Secretary of Commerce and the trade negotiators, they are only insignificant people and we should not pay any attention to them. They are our partners to the agreement and they have set out very clearly in a letter how they interpret the agreement. If that is the case, when our brave Prime Minister met with the Vice-President of the United States yesterday, why did he not say that we have a different interpretation of that agreement and explain our interpretation to him?
The Prime Minister did not say that our interpretation is that once the money is transferred we can spend it as we like. He did not do that because he knows that is not the case. When the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and her officials appeared before the provincial Ministers they were asked how the money could be spent and no answers were given. They said they did not know how the money could be spent. The provinces are now facing total and complete uncertainty. They do not know.
The Parliamentary Secretary has stood in the House and said that it is up to the provinces to decide. How can they decide when the rules of the game are masqueraded? How can they decide whether they can reforest, build a road, or provide worker retraining when the Government has not had the wit, brains, or intelligence to get a fair answer from the Americans as to what is going on? Madam Speaker, is it any wonder that Members on this side have raised some concern and told the people of Canada that they are buying a pig in a poke?
This is a Trojan horse with many hidden implications. The passage of this Bill will be the beginning of the erosion of many of the basic principles about how we run this country. What is at stake is the sovereign right of Canada to price its resources and determine policies for its natural resources as we
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
see fit, and want to do it, not as it is interpreted by the United States Commerce Department, the Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports, or by the President of the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: This agreement allows it.

This agreement says nothing of the kind. The Bill gives the United States the right to obtain all kinds of confidential information. It says that the Minister can provide information to whomever she pleases. She will give it to the Americans.
It is also very clear that the United States has a right to comment upon and be consulted about the calculations of replacement measures. We know full well what will happen when they start trying to impose those replacement measures. If the provinces are required to implement increases in their stumpage fees, it will mean a substantial rise in cost, not just for lumber products exported to the United States but for lumber consumed in Canada and lumber exported to other countries. Rather than being a $600 million Bill, it will be a $1 billion Bill. Therefore, we must conclude that there will not be replacement measures, but we will be stuck with an export duty tax that will become a permanent part of the tax structure of this country.
What will be the consequence of that? Other countries with whom we are competitors in the international market, such as the European Economic Community, will ask why they cannot do the same as the Americans. We have a letter from the Canadian Lumbermen's Association saying sources now report that the Europeans are thinking of imposing an equivalent export tax. The Government has opened a Pandora's box, with a whole series of consequences that it did not know about. The Government cannot tell us about these consequences, yet it expects the House to pass the legislation. That is why it is called a blind trust.
We know how the Government administers blind trusts and we see day after day in the House how the Government and its Ministers go about administering blind trusts for themselves. We do not want a blind trust on the national resources of Canada, which is what this legislation is asking of us.
The Parliamentary Secretary went on to say that the Government signed an agreement that is no different from signing an agreement under GATT. How can the Government be more obtuse than to equate a bilateral trade agreement with a multilateral agreement where there are some 80 other signatories and a whole host of countries defining the rules. As I read into the record of the House yesterday those rules are designed to protect smaller, weaker nations against the imposition of the interest of larger, more powerful nations. One of the purposes of GATT is to set rules to enable large and small countries to exist universally and equally. That is why we have most favoured nation treatment rules.
The federal Government, not only in lumber, but in the larger free trade negotiations, is attempting to sign a bilateral agreement with the most powerful economic nation in the

January 22, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
world, and one that has a very different agenda and a very clear trade interest. Their trade interest is to reduce their trade deficit and they will do it on the backs of their customers, their partners and their allies.
We asked George Bush for the timetable for the trade agreement. He said he could not answer that, which is obvious, because the Americans want to prolong this process for as long as possible since they are the big winners. They win on pharmaceuticals, on books, on fish, on energy, and on softwood lumber. What is next in line? It will be steel, hydroelectric power, potash and all our other resources because the Government has caved in on the fundamental principle, so that the country to our south can now help determine how we set our natural resource policies. That is why the Bill is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I am saddened to speak in this debate now that the Government is trying to choke it off. We have had only a few short hours to relay information to Canadians about what is really happening.
I liken what is happening in this situation to what the United States did in mining the ports in Nicaragua. That small country of Nicaragua had enough gumption to fight in the world court. In our case, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) rose in the House and said that the 15 per cent countervail is an illegal act by the United States which we will begin fighting under GATT. There was a special panel set up to fight and have our interests as a smaller trading nation heard by an international panel.
However, the Secretary of State for External Affairs agreed to have the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) sign a side letter saying that we will not follow this any further with GATT. The United States has done just as it did to Nicaragua in mining their ports. It has mined our forest policy and made it very difficult for small and large companies to operate in any kind of profitable and manageable way in this country.
I want to talk about some of the associated events that led up to this situation and why the Americans were so sure they were dealing with a scatter-brained Government. It is a government that became supinely acquiescent on fish, steel, hogs, raspberries, shakes and shingles, and every other commodity on which the United States wanted to slap some kind of countervail. The Government was mute and did not go to the assistance of those industries.
Let us go back to a meeting in Vancouver where the former Minister of International Trade, the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), was speaking. The U.S. subcommittee on trade was present, on its way to Tokyo. At this meeting, where members of the U.S. Congress and Senate were present, the former Minister offered to amend the Gibbons Bill which was before the U.S. Congress. I was, and I am sure most Canadians were, absolutely flabbergasted to see that kind of simple-minded activity coming from the former Minister for International Trade.
We then saw his replacement, the new Minister for International Trade, go to Washington and make the failed 10 per cent one time only final offer. Within weeks it was jacked up another 50 per cent, despite the fact that the Government itself had gone on public record and said that the countervail duty as it had been put together was illegal. I am not talking only about the double counting, because there must be some kind of criminal activity to have come up with an illegal duty. The Department of Commerce and International Trade Commission was forced to place an illegal 15 per cent countervail against Canada. How did our Government respond? It imposed the 15 per cent export tax against us on our side of the border.
Let me go back a little further. The argument being put forward by Government Members is false and fraudulent in two ways. First, Government Members are saying that this was the lesser of two evils because either the money was going to go into the United States or come to Canada. They are espousing from coast to coast that Parliament should support this because it is better to have money coming to Canada than going to the United States. That is faulty reasoning and I will go back into the history of why it is such a stupid position for Government Members to tell their constituents.
The parallel argument that has been flowing from various Cabinet Ministers' offices to these naive back-benchers is that this $600 million a year will be going back to Canada's forest industries. As my collegue, our critic for international trade, has pointed out, under almost all circumstances that money cannot go back to assist the forest industry. Yesterday Tory Members from British Columbia were saying that this is $400 million of new money for reforestation. Let us think about that for a minute. If Mr. Vander Zalm had been serious when he started skating the feds off the ice and was going to raise stumpage rates as he indicated, that was the time to do so. At that time it would have had significant political impact in the United States. Instead, he is now looking at $400 million as new money. As he has publicly indicated, that money will not go to reforestation or into the forest industry. He will look at his government's priorities for that money. I think it is wrong and despicable for Conservative Members to tell their constituents that this money raised under export tax will be used to assist those workers who are displaced, will go to reforestation, retooling, road construction and to assist those single industry towns that rely on the forest sector. Let me now deal with the posturing taken up by the Minister of Forests of British Columbia, Mr. Kempf and the Premier, Mr. Vander Zalm, as he skated this naive, scatter-brained Government right off the ice. The first statement came early last fall when the Minister of Forests said, of course we are subsidizing. He said it publicly. He said: "We get $150 million revenue from the forest sector and we spend $350 million a year through our forest services". That is a net loss of $200 million. We all know the Socred Government of British Columbia cannot run a pop stand. We have known that for years. However, it managed to finagle its way back into Government.
January 22, 1987

The Premier now has himself a new mandate. He has already skated the feds part way off the ice during the countervailing process last fall. What is the next step he takes? First he says he is going to go it alone to Washington with the Province of Quebec. However, a few quick calls to Premier Bourassa and we learn there have not been too many opportunities, or actual communications between the Premier of British Columbia and the Premier of Quebec, so Premier Vander Zalm abandons that idea after skating the feds even closer to the edge of the ice. Then late in the evening he hears an erroneous radio broadcast in his office. I suppose he had one of those "rocket" radios in his ear. He hears an erroneous news broadcast so he calls a press conference and says a deal has been struck, finally skating the naive feds, this marvellous largest Government in Canadian history, right off the ice, and we see the bureaucrats and the Minister flocking down to Washington to cut a deal on an illegal countervail.
I do not think this House should forget that the countervail duty was illegal. It was illegally composed mathematically and the findings which were made were illegal. We are the largest trading partner the United States has. Ontario alone has a larger trade balance with the United States than does Japan. It is amazing that our largest trading ally is bullying us in this way because of protectionist sentiments in the United States.
Let me now really deal with the issue. Industry had an opportunity and it now realizes the effects of allowing the Government to do it. As Adam Zimmerman put it, it was like allowing the orderly in the hospital to do the heart surgery, the five-way bypass. We have seen how this Government has mismanaged from start to finish.
I went down to Washington almost two years ago with Hon. Members of the House who were interested in this issue. We took the pulse of protectionism and found out the affect the U.S. coalition was having on elected representatives in the United States. We found they were very effective. Our Ambassador, Mr. Gotlieb, a very intelligent and well informed man, was well aware of where this issue was starting to move. He had certain ideas which I brought back to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), as did other members of that delegation.
We pointed out we had to get to U.S. consumers. The U.S. consumers know this will increase the cost of a house in the United States between SI,000 and $4,000 U.S. That is very likely going to bring about a further reduction in housing starts in the United States. We are lucky right now because there is a bit of a blip in the United States because interest rates are down and people are still buying homes. However, the fact is that the culmination of this export tax, with anything like the 1982 reduction in demand for Canadian SPF products, is going to have devastating consequences, particularly for small mills, and, if Mr. Widman is correct, to a far greater extent in eastern Canada than in western Canada, in part due to the nature of stumpage policies in this country. If
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
one compares British Columbia and the Maritimes, one finds that the Maritimes pay six times the stumpage fees now paid in most of British Columbia.
That brings me to the point where again members of the Government say that these hundreds of millions of dollars are going to be converted into stumpage increases, and so on. There is no incentive now for Mr. Vander Zalm or Mr. Kempf, or for the B.C. Government, to increase the stumpage rates in British Columbia because of the bottle-neck which will be created with the Department of Commerce, first, and also the fact that they receive fluid cash every month from Ottawa under the export tax which they can spend on ferries, roads, or whatever kind of nicknacks the provincial Government decides is politically popular.
I would like to end my remarks with the point of this whole exercise. We should have gone to the United States consumers, not as Parliamentarians, not as a forest industry, but through trade consulates in the United States, as all countries which have an evolving, mature relationship with the United States do. Finally, this whole issue revolves around the fact that the American forest industry is using this as a means to fix prices. It is going through this whole conundrum to fix prices in the United States, to drive them up. We should all remember that ITNT were the ones who drafted the resource pricing section of Sam Gibbons' Bill. They are after our forest lands and our industry with a vengeance. We should have stood up stronger and more firmly as a country and fought this to the ground before it ever got to the countervailing duty stage.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I had a few minutes to speak earlier this afternoon and I was hoping that at that time I had made a convincing enough argument that all Conservative Members would want to change their vote. However, as you know, being a nonpartisan person sitting in that chair, and being able to evaluate these things, obviously these Tories need a bit more convincing. So let me try it one more time.
Very eloquently.

My colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) says "very eloquently", but these Tories are stubborn. We have to explain this point again and again to the Conservative Government.
What we have before us in Bill C-37 is not an issue involving only softwood lumber. Of course it is that, but as I said earlier this afternoon, we are talking about sovereignty, our country. We are talking about relinquishing and surrendering some of our rights, the rights of a sovereign nation, to another country.
This is indeed precedent setting. What we have to ask ourselves is why we are doing it. If it were the proper thing to do, if there were no other alternatives, it would still be wrong to relinquish our sovereignty in this way. But it was not the only thing to do. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) could have stood up to the President instead of being busy kissing his

Mr. Speaker, that is why Canadians no longer trust this minister. That is why they no longer trust this government which could not stand on its own two feet.
The Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Cadieux), who represents the riding next to mine and who sits on Government benches, certainly knows that his Prime Minister has surrendered part of our sovereignty to the Americans when he introduced that legislation. Some might argue that he did not do it himself, but that his Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) who spends her time in Hawaii did it, and they would be right.
I should like the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil to tell me who appointed the Hawaiian minister? Well, it was the Prime Minister, and you know, Mr. Speaker, as we all know now, that it was a poor choice.
We know that we should now ask the Minister responsible for International Trade to move somewhere else, to do something else, perhaps warm up one of the back-benches over there, and to ask one of the Hon. Members who do not speak
often, for I am sure that among all of them, there are at least one or two who are able to speak-I am not really sure of that, for I have not seen any of them open their mouths yet-but because of the law of probability, I am sure some of them could speak.
I am sure also that the Hon. Member for Beauharnois- Salaberry (Mr. Hudon) who represents the riding situated to the South-East of mine, could speak in the House, and that as a Minister, he could do just as good a job as the current Minister. He could certainly not do worse than she.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that my friend and neighbour would at least try to defend the interests of Canadians. His riding runs along the American border, so that he is well aware of the influence and size of that neighbouring country.

We are not discussing here whether the United States is a friendly or unfriendly neighbour. Of course it is a friendly neighbour. That is not the issue. I have friendly neighbours of my own. That does not mean that they are allowed to enter my house and run away with everything that is there. The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) has his office right next to mine. I consider him to be a friendly neighbour.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Have you noticed we always close our doors?

He does not enter my office and run away with my furniture, which is precisely what the Government is proposing in this Bill. It is offering a means by which someone will be able to decide whether or not what we are doing in our country is right. They will not even have to come here to do it. They will be able to stay at home in Washington and tell us from there whether or not we are governing a small aspect of our country in the proper way.
Some may say that this issue alone is not relinquishing totally the sovereignty of our country-perhaps not. But it is a foot in the door. It is very clearly a decision aimed in that direction.
As I said at the opening of my remarks, this was done erroneously. Most Canadians believe that had the case gone through the proper adjudication methods we would have won, as we have in the past. Members opposite say: "We won in the past but the process started again, therefore we did not really win at all because we won and then a couple of years later the Americans started threatening us again with a countervail". That is fine. What is there to say that they will not start again the day after we pass this Bill? What is there to say that they will not ask that the 15 per cent be increased to 35 per cent, or whatever? How are we to know? In the past we wanted what we felt was right, and we did so for the right reasons. However, the Americans came back to us demanding that things be changed.
I say to the silent Tories, those who form the silent majority, those who never say a word in the House other than to holler the odd heckle, that there will be a day when they will have to speak up. It is fine for them not to stand in their places, not to
January 22, 1987

speak on behalf of their constituents. However, some day they will have to return to their constituents and be accountable. Their constituents will say to them: "Where were you when the softwood lumber issue was being discussed?" They will have to say that they were sitting in the back row watching members of the Opposition speak. That will not be good enough. Their constituents will not accept that. They will turf them out of office the next time around and put the Liberals back in.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might be permitted to put on the record the facts which face us in this country. I would like to limit my remarks to facts. I do not want to enter into rhetoric, attempts to destroy personalities and individuals, attacks on the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) which are strictly out of character in this House. However, it is not something which is out of character for members of the Liberal Party or members of the New Democratic Party.
Let us consider the facts. Some two years ago a dispute developed with respect to softwood lumber entering the United States. The Americans wanted to impose a countervail. What happened? The case went before a tribunal and Canada won.
Just two years later another fact emerged. The climate in the United States was such that the Americans were becoming protectionists. There were something in the order of 300 Bills in Congress alone which proposed to bar imports from other countries. A real protectionist mood has developed in the United States. We all know that. Every Member sitting in the House knows that.
So it is fact that a dispute developed. Members of the lumber industry in the United States approached their Congressmen and Senators and said: "We want a countervail. We want you to impose a 15 per cent duty". That was done, it was not just proposed. A 15 per cent duty was imposed on the import of softwood lumber coming from Canada to the United States. Where did that money go? It went straight into the Treasury of the United States. That is where it went. By the way, that was only an interim solution. The lumber industry down there said that the hurt it was feeling was closer to the equivalent of 25 per cent and that is a fact.
Thus the process started. What was going to happen? We were to appear before a tribunal. Members opposite say that if we had fought the situation right through we probably would have won the case. I want to tell Members opposite that the whole situation in the United States has changed. The temper has changed. The best judgment of the government experts we consulted was that this was not going to happen. We were told that we probably would lose.
The other side of the coin is that, even if we did win it would take four years to do so, during which time the 15 per cent would still be in place and going directly to the Treasury of the United States. That is a fact. If we were able to win the case, which could have happened, then there was nothing in place to stop the United States with their protectionist attitude from
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
coming in with legislation and imposing the 15 per cent anyway. Our best judgment told us to strike a deal with the United States so that we could keep those funds in Canada. The important issue was to keep the money in Canada. With that money, we can assist with the problems that may face the industry. That is a fact.
The other fact that everyone glosses over or does not allude to is that after the agreement was signed the stocks of all of the softwood lumber industry went up very dramatically on the Toronto Stock and the Vancouver Stock Exchanges. Not only did the stocks go up, but the price of lumber to the consumer in the United States went up approximately 13 per cent. This means that all that happened is that the price of lumber has gone up in the United States market, and the consumer in the United States is paying the 15 per cent difference that is being collected for the Canadian Treasury.
The money will be put into a special fund. That fund will be passed to the provinces proportionately. The provinces will determine how this money will be handled, whether it is spent on silviculture or reforestation. Those are the facts that, when speaking on behalf of our constituents, all Members on this side of the House have expressed time and time again.
What do we hear from the Liberal-NDP coalition? We hear nothing but character assassination of the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). We hear nothing but innuendo and character assassination of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), and of every member of this Government who states the facts. They do not wish to listen to the facts. What they wish to do is malign and carry on a fractious House, and say things in the House that they would never admit to saying if they walked out on to the street. They would never admit to saying some of the garbage that they try to throw in the form of debate. It is not debate, it is a rat pack mentality that has taken over with the Liberals, and the NDP are falling into line like the lemmings heading to the sea; one lemming starts and all the rest follow. That is the way it works.
I would like to talk about the sovereignty issue and the types of things that are being mentioned. We heard the Member, who calls himself my neighbour, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), say that we lost sovereignty. I heard the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) talk about sovereignty. I also heard the NDP talk about sovereignty, and how we have given it away. When two people have a dispute and those people come to an agreement, they agree to do certain things. They both lose a little bit of their free choice. In the dispute to resolve the dispute, each side has to give a little bit.
In the truest sense, there are certain things that we cannot do with the 15 per cent tax that we will be collecting, but we have agreed to that. The United States Government has said that it wishes to monitor what we do, because it is not sure that we will not give it to some of our producers of softwood lumber

January 22, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
through the back door. That is a reasonable thing. But we have also extracted from the United States Government that it, in turn, will not come back in on a countervail and break the agreement; that it will live with a 15 per cent export tax, and not come after it again. So we have solved the lumber dispute. They have given up the sovereignty that we extracted from them, because that is the nature of bilateral agreements. Every bilateral agreement signed between governments means that each government has to give up something to make that bilateral agreement work. All Members in this House know that to be true. And all Members of this House, if they were acting responsibly, would stand in their place and say so, and cut out this foolishness and garbage that they are throwing in as an obstruction.
We have other business to attend to in the House, to make sure that the Government and the people in Canada are getting what they put us here to do, that is, to give them proper Government. Interest rates are falling. We have economic problems to face. We have unemployment. We have many things to be addressed in the House. Most importantly, we have freedom to move legislation that will, once and for all, remove the freight rate inequity between western and eastern Canada. We want to get this on the board and discuss it. We want to get it into committee and pass it, so we can equalize the opportunities across this country. We have the good old socialist NDP and Liberal coalition doing everything they can to obstruct action in the House. I wish to put on record that I resent that attitude. I hope that they will be men enough to stand in their place and say what a good deal we have received in this trade war.

Mr. Speaker, the last speaker, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), talked about character assassination. He said that our side was interested in character assassination. We are not interested in character assassination as far as the Conservative Party is concerned, because they are committing suicide with their own characters. We just need to watch them. Day after day they are involved in a suicidal mission, as far as their characters are concerned, so there is no need for assassination.
The Hon. Member stated that he wished to put some facts on the table. I would also like to place a few facts on the table. The first fact is that the Tory Government is trying to stifle debate on this issue. There are Members on this side of the House who have more things they wish to say, some important facts that we wish to put on the table. We also believe that there are some back-benchers in the Tory caucus who have some things to say, if they can wait long enough to get up the gumption to stand up on their hind legs and say it.
When I had a chance to speak a couple of days ago I outlined some of the history of bungling that has characterized the way that this Government has mismanaged the entire free trade relationship with the United States. Nevertheless, the Minister claims that she won a victory when she reached this deal in the dying days of 1986. She claims it was a victory. It
reminded me of the Battle of Blenheim where a couple of small children, 50 years after the battle, find a skull. They asked their old grandfather to tell them all about the war, and what they fought each other for. "That I cannot say," said he, but it was a famous victory. I can imagine some child 50 years from now finding an old newspaper and looking at it and asking to be told all the softwood facts, and how we got the export tax. "That I cannot say," said she, "but it was a famous victory," with just the odd anomaly. The Minister had to admit that there are a few anomalies in this agreement. There are a few people who should have been protected who are not.
Whatever victory the Minister might have found in this agreement, most of us fear that if we have two or three more victories like that, there will be precious little of our sovereignty left. Is this the type of victory that the Government is looking for in the whole free trade negotiations with the United States? I very much fear that this is the type of victory that we might end up with, an agreement in which we get the short end of the stick and the Government stands up and states that we won a great victory. The end result of this victory is that workers will pay for it with the loss of their jobs.
Yesterday, there was an IWA study released in British Columbia which indicated that from their point of view they thought that British Columbia would be able to weather the storm not too badly in the short term. I hope that they are correct. I hope the facts that at present the American consumers are absorbing the greatest percentage of the tax; that at the present time there is a buoyant housing market in the United States; and that most of our mills in British Columbia are fairly technologically competent means that we will be able to weather this storm with a minimum of further disruption to our economy. The forest industry in British Columbia has suffered a great deal. It cannot afford to suffer more.
I talked to an IWA official who said that even though they do not anticipate any massive lay-offs, this deal means that there will not be the anticipated and hoped for recovery of the economy. There will be no third shifts put on at mills that have been barely staying open. Even in British Columbia where they think it will not have that much of a negative impact, it will certainly dampen any hopes for recovery.
Even if British Columbia is not as heavily hit in the short term, at least three other factors need to be taken into consideration. First, there is the long-term implications for British Columbia. If the U.S. market is buoyant right now, what will happen when there is a downturn? We know that there are upturns and downturns in the U.S. housing market. When that happens American consumers will not be absorbing the increased costs. This means that Canadian manufacturers will have to absorb them. They will have to lower their price to export to the American market.
Can the Canadian lumber industry absorb an increased cost of $500 million or $600 million per year? In effect, that is their profit right now. It would mean that they would have to
January 22, 1987

operate at a loss or without any profit. It would also mean that they would have to reduce prices to sell to the American market. Then the question would be, are we to have a two-price system for exports? Are we to expect that the Japanese will let us export to the United States at a lower price while they pay a 15 per cent higher price? Of course not. The lower price they will have to absorb for the United States market will have to apply to other importers of our softwood. That sort of thing will hit British Columbia woodworkers hard in the long term.
Second, we must look at the effects on other parts of Canada. The Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) spoke about this very eloquently on Monday when he asked for an emergency debate. As reported at page 2346 of Hansard, he said:
My request under Standing Order 29 is based on the recent decision to impose a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber which has caused grave concern among Maritime lumber producers. Many producers fear for the economic viability of their operations, and the jobs dependent upon their competitiveness.
The agreement imposes the tax upon all but five Maritime softwood producers that previously enjoyed exemptions from such action. The consequence of such a decision creates a situation whereby the livelihood of Maritime softwood producers is threatened by an action designed to resolve a problem created by extremely low stumpage fees in British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, and Quebec.
Many lumber producers fear that they will not survive if they are required to pay not only the highest stumpage fees in Canada, but also an additional 15 per cent tax on their exported products. There is also a very real concern that the lumber market within the Maritime provinces may be swamped by western lumber seeking refuge from the tax.
These were the comments of the Conservative back-bencher who was speaking out of concern for what the Bill would do to his constituents and to his region. I commend him for having the gumption to stand and raise these concerns in the face of a Government which does not seem to care.
Third, we must look at the effect of this 15 per cent export tax and the deal reached with the Americans on other industries. I am not referring only to the softwood lumber industry but to the pulp industry, for example. In many provinces the stumpage rates for pulp and lumber are the same. If the softwood lumber export tax is replaced by increased stumpage fees, it will mean increased costs for pulp mills. In turn, it will be very difficult for some of those operations to continue.
The total effect will be that small communities will be devastated and jobs will be lost. Many single industry towns across the nation depend upon the lumber industry, but the Government has no plans in place to help them.
Finally, we see this deal as a way of giving away our sovereignty. I am reminded of the words of an old poem:
Ours is a sovereign nation Bows to no foreign will
But whenever they cough in Washington They spit on Parliament Hill.

their graves. One hundred and twenty years after Confederation the Conservative Government is giving away the Canadian sovereignty for which they built this nation. Sir John A. Macdonald would not be very proud of the gang which now occupies the seats of Government.

We hear great statements that trees are beautiful, and they are, that trees are useful, and they are. We hear all kinds of things about conservation and the wealth of our forests, one of the greatest assets of our nation, and jobs. How often have we heard the term "jobs"? Since when is fish a crop?

The Hon. Member asks since when fish has been a crop. Fish are a crop. People grow fish today. Why are trees a crop? People thought it was foolish to speak of trees as a crop. Forests are located on private lands, Crown lands and parklands. We are not just talking about forestry costs in this agreement. We are not just talking about stumpage fees because that 15 per cent goes on the initial cost of the timber, its milling, the wages, compensation costs, equipment costs and the trucking costs, until it reaches the border at 15 per cent. That 15 per cent tax does not increase our stumpage fees in Canada but taxes labour, our sawmills and processing mills in Canada.
There is a large lumber mill in my area that sells to a wholesaler in Ottawa, which also sells to an Alexandria moulding company in eastern Ontario. When it sells its product it is still paying 15 per cent. Let us assume that the cost to the moulding company is 30 per cent for its equipment and wages to produce the moulding. fact that the Government is proposing a 15 per cent duty on our wood products in Canada at the request of the United States is evidence of internal interference and the practical beginning of commercial union. Adam Zimmerman was right when he said that the Government sold out.

Let us consider the cost of wood, for example. Because of the great demand for pine, it costs far more for the additional work in producing the various sizes in lumber than it does to produce hemlock which has a very small profit margin. A 15

per cent tax on hemlock will result in a smaller demand that will result in less product in the sawmills. The Government that talked so much about jobs in the last election is, in effect, taxing the very jobs that exist.
Some timber rights in Ontario are more than 100 years old. People who own those timber rights spend a lot of money on reforestation and road maintenance. Yet they are being taxed for managing that forest.

Madam Speaker, I am really glad I have a chance to make a few remarks on this very important Bill which has extreme implications for many people in Canada, particularly for the one million forest workers. I would like to say that I meet from time to time with many of the forestry workers and those people who are related to the forest industry in my riding of Vancouver East. For a
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
long time we have been very concerned about the forestry policy in British Columbia, or the lack of policy, I should say. I mention this because I think the background is quite important to this Bill.
I think the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) outlined from a historical perspective that for many years the Social Credit Government has really refused to look at what was happening to our forests in British Columbia. I think most Hon. Members would agree that we have the most beautiful forests in the world. Yet we have had our hillsides stripped and there has been really no government policy which has been effective in replacing those trees. This means that we are really selling out our future. The federal and provincial Governments from time to time have talked about reforestation and silviculture but they have done very little in this respect. We had hoped when the Conservative Government came into office it would appoint a senior Minister of Forestry and perhaps that person would mean we were finally going to get some real action in developing a sound forestry and reforestation policy. However, we have a very junior Minister and one from whom we have heard only a little, I am sad to say.
As to the lumber export tax, I think it is such a complicated process and policy that it is unfortunate the Government has chosen to try to stifle debate. I was astounded to hear from my colleagues that once again the Government is really trying to push this Bill through and in effect impose closure. It is important that we get all the facts. I would like to have a chance to do much more research and get more views as to the projected effects not just of the lumber export tax but of the whole precedence which has been set in place in the way this international incident, if you like, has been handled.
I think most of us on this side of the House, and I hope I can include the Hon. Members at either end when I say this, would agree that there has been really a lousy process of negotiation with the United States on this issue from beginning to end. We have been intimidated and have fluctuated back and forth. We have not been consistent. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that the negotiations are not over yet. I would be very interested to see how the Government and the Minister makes out in trying to resolve many of the interprovincial policies with which she will be faced when this Bill goes through.
I am sure, as my colleagues have been saying tonight, that we negotiated from a position of weakness. That is very unfortunate. As I was coming out of my office this evening, I overheard one of the speakers saying it is absolutely appalling that the Minister could not take a sound and strong position. She probably should not have got involved in the first place. There are those who feel this should have been left to the courts. However, once she did get involved, the kind of inconsistency, which really weakened her whole position, and in turn weakened Canada's negotiating position, is well known and well documented. She offered 10 per cent as a final offer. I think she said two or three times she was making a final offer. Then, of course, she backed down and went up to 15 per cent.

January 22, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I must say, I feel a little sorry for the Minister because I am sure during this process she was not assisted at all by the interference of our Premier of British Columbia. He just could not keep his nose out of it. It was not at that stage a provincial question. It was part of federal negotiations. I think it was most important that he be sensitive to the whole free trade negotiations. The role of the provinces is to work in collaboration through the federal Government, not to intervene, compete and grandstand and try to take over in place of the federal Government. There was an election and a post-election period and the Premier of British Columbia wanted to be a hero. I wonder what kind of a hero he has turned out to be? What he did was create a situation where he is an embarrassment to us. I understand he was in the United States in this last week or so. I hate to think of what kind of things are now being negotiated behind our backs.
We have heard about a lot of the issues. I know I will be repeating some of them but I would like to put some of them on the record. The first and probably the most important issue, aside from the process I have already mentioned, is the implications that this whole incident has had, and will continue to have, on Canada's sovereignty. The United States now has the power to intervene and influence the forest policy of Canada. That is a very bad precedent for free trade negotiations generally.
I want to mention again what my Hon. Leader said when he spoke on this issue. He said with reference to the issue of sovereignty that the agreement contains the following words: Calculation of the value of any replacement measures in relation to the export charge will be subject to further consultations and agreement between the two Governments. Canada's fiscal and forestry policies will be subject to further consultations and agreement between the two Governments.
The word "agreement" is not an ambiguous word. If a provincial Government replaces the export tax with increased stumpage or other charges, it will have to obtain the agreement of the United States Government. I agree with our Leader. Certainly that would appear to be the case. He goes on to say that we are now involved in any change in implementing the replacement of the 15 per cent at the provincial level with the provinces having to go to the federal Government, and the federal Government having to trot down to Washington to say: "Will you please agree with us because if you do not, we cannot do it".
I think that any way one looks at it, it is a deplorable situation that we are losing such face and such control over our own forest industry. It is even more important that this is a precedent which will affect our total negotiations and our relationship with the United States, not to mention with other countries. If this example is effective with the United States, what are our friends in GATT and the European Market going to say to us?
We know that sovereignty is one of the very major concerns and sovereignty is a federal responsibility. Some of my colleagues in British Columbia do not care as much about the
sovereignty issue. They are concerned with the forest industry primarily. As federal politicians that is our responsibility. We are Members of Parliament. We have a Government that is in charge of all the external relationships of Canada. It is responsible for protecting our sovereignty. I do not think it has done a good job at all in this case.

subtopic: AIR CANADA-EMPLOYEES' PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR FULL ANNUAL REPORTS
AIR CANADA-EMPLOYEES' PENSION PLAN-REQUEST FOR FULL ANNUAL REPORTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, late in November I had the opportunity to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) a question concerning the availability of pension fund information for Air Canada employees. I had received some inquiries from a few constituents of Fraser Valley East who were worried that excess pension funds may be used incorrectly.
After examining the issue and after having the opportunity to question officials of Air Canada, I have found that instead of excess funds in the Air Canada pension fund there is actually an unfunded liability of some $248 million. This figure is readily available from the Public Accounts, 1985-86, which is published by the Receiver General.
This unfunded liability is not a problem, however, since it is very closely monitored by actuaries. The actuarial studies are done over a 30-year period and the funding is being handled by annual payments over various periods ending in 2003. The actuaries ensure that a stream of payments exists that will eventually eradicate the unfunded liability and change the payments to meet the needs of the fund. The apparent lack of information about the pension fund experienced by some pensioners could be a result of misinterpretation of the actual details.
The Air Canada pension fund is based on a final earnings plan which means that the employees' pensions are guaranteed to the maximum, regardless of anything. The employer must meet that obligation. Since 1973, Air Canada has increased the pensions yearly, but this is done on an ad hoc basis, not by indexation. Ad hoc calculations include many important factors such as review of inflation, an examination of other large pension funds, ability to pay and community influences. In many cases this method actually gives the pensioner a higher increase than an indexed pension.
January 22, 1987

The Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985, which came into effect on January 1, 1987, includes a number of measures to try to further ensure the financial solvency of federally-regulated pension plans. The PBSA sets minimum standards for pension plans established by companies in federally-regulated industries, such as Air Canada which is a parent Crown corporation.
Because of this Act pension plan administrators will have a statutory obligation to administer the pension fund to protect the benefit of plan members.
In his recent report the Auditor General stated that "the viability of pension plans is of vital importance to Canadians". He recommended, to further protect the interests of Canadians, that independent reviews must be carried out by the Department of Insurance, which regulates all federally-registered employee pension plans. At this time the Department supervises some 750 plans, covering 600,000 employees. As can be seen this is a huge workload. According to the Auditor General there is the risk, that the present supervisory procedure of the Pension Benefits Division will not permit it to do an adequate job of monitoring the financial solvency of all employee pension plans.
He recommends that the Department of Insurance should undertake a thorough review of its present supervisory practices for pension plans. In particular, the Auditor General recommends that it should review the adequacy of procedures for monitoring pension plan assets.
The Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985, will no doubt give the final assurance that federally-regulated pension plans maintain minimum standards. The Public Accounts of the Receiver General continue to provide the public with information on the financial statements of Crown corporations such as Air Canada. The information from the Public Accounts Report is used to write the company's annual report.
On a more local level, Air Canada pensioners are well served by representatives across Canada. These people keep in close contact with Air Canada's head office.
At this time, Air Canada could not do anything with the pension funds, in terms of investing or selling out, because not only is it against the law to take funds out when there is an unfunded liability, but the unfunded liability would increase. Finally, close actuarial control does not allow this to happen in any case.
In closing, I appreciate having this chance to address the House, but particularly to be able to report to the people of Fraser Valley East on this matter. They must not only be reassured that there are not any excess funds in the Air Canada pension fund but that there is not any reason to be concerned about the unfunded liability either.

PORTS-VANCOUVER-REQUEST FOR FUNDS TO UPGRADE FACILITIES. (B) REQUEST THAT PORT USERS COMMITTEE BE ESTABLISHED
speechtext:
I wish to speak to the question that 1 raised in the House on November 17, 1986, relating to the Port of Vancouver. There are some very urgent problems faced at the Port of Vancouver. It desperately needs upgraded facilities in order to be competitive.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) was asked by me for an assurance that the federal Government would take some positive action that would not just be a reaction to the management-labour crisis at that time, but would really help with the port's long-term development. First was that there would be an upgrading of port facilities, particularly three new cranes that are very badly needed. There should also be improved rail facilities in order to be competitive with the American rail facilities which largely accommodate container traffic.
Second, we asked that they establish a port users committee, or that they work with the Vancouver group to establish a committee to seriously assess the problems, the solutions, and the priorities to ensure the long-term viability and competitiveness of the Port of Vancouver. I asked this question when the labour dispute was at a peak when the Maritime Employers' Council had locked out the ILWU from the Port of Vancouver. Unfortunately, this ended with some very harsh legislation brought down by the federal Government, which we are still

January 22, 1987
Adjournment Debate
very concerned about because it threatened the collective bargaining rights in that jurisdiction.
Unfortunately, the Deputy Prime Minister was so absorbed with the labour dispute that he failed to provide an adequate answer to my question. This is very typical of both Liberal and Conservative Governments. They only seem to become interested in the Port of Vancouver, which is away out on the Pacific West Coast, when there is a crisis, and when that crisis usually involves labour troubles. In this case it was management that had imposed the lock-out. They ignore the long-term problems.
The dispute in the port at that time was a symptom of much greater problems facing the port. We must find a way of dealing with those. Unfortunately the labour dispute drew much attention from the media and the Government. It was based upon the so-called container clause which allows union members to unpack containers and load their contents on to trucks or railway cars, if the contents are consigned to more than one owner within a certain radius of the port. It is designed to protect jobs for a certain number of longshore workers.
However, it is important to note that it affects only 12.6 per cent of inbound containers through the port, a relatively small amount of port traffic. Yet the powers that be, and even the port administration, treated the issue as the primary problem facing the port.
Years of neglect under both Liberal and Conservative Governments have helped to erode the viability of the Port of Vancouver. It should be developed. It has the potential to be developed into a competitive world-class port. It is a wonderful location. We have the needed skilled workers, industries and so on, but we need a method of bringing together all these parts in a comprehensive way to do some long-term planning and improvements.
This is why I supported the port awareness campaign sponsored by the longshoremen's union, the ILWU. It is called "a world-class port for a world-class city". It offers positive solutions to the port's serious problems. It is important to congratulate such groups when they are working on the positive, long range side of things.
First and foremost, the Port of Vancouver needs genuine local autonomy. The Ports Corporation Act, in which I recall being very involved a few years ago, was passed by the Liberals. It was supposed to develop autonomy in ports, particularly in the Port of Vancouver. However, there are still far too many "made in Ottawa" decisions.
The Board of Directors of the Vancouver Port Corporation is comprised of political appointees. It was the Liberal Government which set up that structure, so it is not surprising that the present Government has carried through on it. Although these members undoubtedly work hard and are genuinely concerned about the affairs of the port, they are
influenced by Ottawa and by the agenda of the Conservative Government. It is difficult for them to be concerned about all the various factions involved in the entire operation and the future of the port. It is not their fault; as I say, it is the structure.
The first step on the road to a more responsive and autonomous management of the port would be to establish a port users committee as was outlined. This committee should include shippers, key users of the port, railways, unions, surrounding communities, local levels of Government, the grain industry, and so on. It should help to study the Port of Vancouver and to develop a long-range plan as well as deal with immediate problems.
We have a serious problem competing with the Pacific northwest. If we do not have a better, improved railway system, we will not be able to take the container traffic eastward or back and forth across Canada. It will continue to go through the American routes.
I am sorry that my time is almost up, but again I urge the Deputy Prime Minister to take another look at the matter. He has a good background in the whole transportation field. We urge both him and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to support strongly the establishment of a port users committee, to ensure that funds are available for at least three more cranes, and to bring all parties together to see whether we can have an improved Port of Vancouver.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PORTS-VANCOUVER-REQUEST FOR FUNDS TO UPGRADE FACILITIES. (B) REQUEST THAT PORT USERS COMMITTEE BE ESTABLISHED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with respect to the establishment of a port users committee for the Port of Vancouver, I point out to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) that a regional advisory council was established for ports on the West Coast in April, 1983. As I am sure the Hon. Member knows, the council advises and makes recommendations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) on matters related to ports in the region. These involve regional interests and concerns relative to port development, land-use planning, transportation, economic and environmental issues.
The membership of the Western Regional Advisory Council, I am told, includes the chairmen of harbour commissions in the region, the chairmen of the local port corporations in the region, including Vancouver and Prince Rupert, a representative of the Department of Transport, two representatives of the Province of British Columbia, a representative from each of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba and various industry representatives.
Over and above the requirements of the legislation, the Vancouver Port Corporation itself has established continuous communication with the Western Transportation Advisory Council, which include governments, producers and shippers, ports, labour, carriers and trade associations; the Vancouver Board of Trade, the Longshoremen's Union, the Maritime Employers' Association, each of the adjacent municipalities,
January 22, 1987

the Chamber of Shipping, the Council of Forest Industries, the Wharf Operators' Association, the Canadian International Freight Forwarders Association and the Economic Development Ministers of the four western provinces.
In addition, the Vancouver Port Corporation Board has always included a senior representative from labour. Currently, Mr. Jack Munro of the International Woodworkers' of America serves on the board as successor to Mr. Don Garcia who is currently President of the Canadian area of the ILWU representing the longshoremen on the West Coast.
Second, with respect to facilities at the Port of Vancouver, I am pleased to advise this House and the Member that the Port of Vancouver has invested in excess of $75 million since 1983, including approximately $33 million directly and indirectly related to container handling and distribution.
Present operational container crane and shore-side equipment has the capacity to handle an estimated 325,000, 20-foot equivalent units per year. This will be substantially increased when terminally handling equipment now on order by the terminal contractors becomes operational in mid-1987. The through-put in 1986 was 222,781 20-foot equivalent units, thus indicating that Vancouver already has additional capacity in excess of 100,000 20-foot equivalent units annually.
Finally, the Vancouver Port Corporation has estimated its capital requirements over the next five years to be $75 million, which will be funded from port operations. This includes provision for additional container handling equipment as demand develops.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REFUGEES-DEPORTATION OF IRANIAN FROM UNITED STATES. (B) REQUEST FOR ISSUANCE OF MINISTERIAL PERMIT
REFUGEES-DEPORTATION OF IRANIAN FROM UNITED STATES. (B) REQUEST FOR ISSUANCE OF MINISTERIAL PERMIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this evening to review a question that I asked the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) in the House last December, 1986. The question involves the case of one Mr. Moatanedi, a 25 year-old Iranian student who is presently in the United States pending deportation to Iran.
The question of the matter revolves around the issue that the Canadian Government does not wish to extend a hand of humanity to this one individual who faces certain persecution and probably death as soon as he touches the tarmac in Iran.
There is a community in eastern Canada in the Province of Nova Scotia that is willing to sponsor this individual. There are individuals across Canada who have written and phoned the Minister over the course of the last two months. We have a policy where we recruit some 12,000 refugees from around the world. We have 6,000 additional refugees who are supported and sponsored by communities in Canada. We have ministerial permits that are granted to individuals who merit special consideration because of their special circumstances, and yet we have this one individual who is looking to Canada for assistance and looking to Canada to stay his eventual departure from the United States, a deportation that was already attempted once. En route to Iran the plane stopped in Paris
Adjournment Debate
and Mr. Moatanedi tried to commit suicide as opposed to facing death in Iran. The French returned him to the United States, the Americans did not even blink and are prepared to put him on a plane for the second time in under a year.
My questions to the Minister were simply why the Government was not allowing Canadians and the community of Yarmouth to sponsor this individual and give the green light. If the Government did not wish to allow a community or a group of individuals to sponsor this man why could the Minister not find something within his department to extend a special ministerial permit, given the very special circumstances of this 25 year-old.
My office was in touch with this individual's lawyer in Washington today and she confirmed for the record once again that this individual is still in hospital in Washington waiting for Canada to extend its arms to him if the United States maintains its original position.
At the time I asked the Minister the question, he gave me a number of reasons why he could not do it, why the individual was not a bona fide refugee and why his papers were not in order. The answers to those questions were certainly inadequate. I look forward to hearing the Parliamentary Secretary provide Canadians, and particularly the sponsors in eastern Canada, with an update as to where the Government stands vis-a-vis Mr. Moatanedi's case and what he can look forward to if anything at all from Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFUGEES-DEPORTATION OF IRANIAN FROM UNITED STATES. (B) REQUEST FOR ISSUANCE OF MINISTERIAL PERMIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to add to the reply given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) on December 1.
As the Hon. Member is aware, Mr. Moatamedi was admitted to the United States in 1978 at the age of 17 as a foreign student. In 1981, he married an American citizen and held a job in that country until his student visa expired in the summer of 1984. On his return from Mexico in the fall of 1984, he was apprehended by the United States Immigration Services and he asked for asylum in that country at the hearing to review his deportation order. He was later refused asylum in the United States and a deportation order against him was maintained in April 1986 to force him to return to Iran.
His desperate act during a stopover in Paris postponed his return to Iran since the French authorities decided to send him back to the United States where he has since been detained in a psychiatric centre.
As the Hon. Member already knows, the case of this man has been reviewed in depth by Canadian visa officers in Washington to determine whether he could be admitted to Canada as a refugee under the terms of the convention. For the information of the House, both Canada and the United

January 22, 1987
Adjournment Debate
States are signatory countries of the 1951 Geneva Convention on refugee status and the related 1967 Protocol. The visa officers evaluated the request of Mr. Moatamedi, but based on the individual merits of this case, it was established that his claim for refugee status was unfounded.
As you already know, the Minister of State for Immigration subsequently refused Mr. Moatamedi a ministerial permit which would have admitted him to Canada since there were not sufficient humanitarian reasons to justify such a claim as this case was under the jurisdiction of the American authorities. The United States Immigration Services have continued to pressure for the deportation of Mr. Moatamedi and had been expecting to expel him from the United States as early as January 7, 1987. However, in the meantime, there have been two major developments which could allow the American authorities to reverse their stand in favour of Mr. Moatamedi. First, the representative in Canada of the United States High Commission for Refugees advised Mr. Weiner on December 31, 1986, that his organization had decided to grant Mr. Moatamedi refugee status under the terms of the Convention because of all the publicity his case had received in Canada. The representative of this organization in the United States confirmed his agreement with this decision and so informed the lawyer of the claimant who then requested that United
States Immigration Appeal Commission defer execution of the deportation order of her client.
Mr. Moatamedi's lawyer is expected to submit to this Board an application for review in order for this applicant's case to be presented again to the U.S. Immigration and, for this purpose, she will advise the board members of the decision rendered by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees that Mr. Moatamedi is now deemed by the representatives of this organization in the United States to be a refugee under the convention.
We are waiting for a final decision from the United States Immigration Appeal Board and we hope that the decision rendered by the High Commissioner will bring about a favourable solution to this matter which continues to come under the American authorities.
